history.heading: Medieval Bosnia
paragraphs: The region was inhabited by Illyrian tribes and later became part of the Roman Empire. Slavs settled there in the 6th and 7th centuries. A Bosnian state emerged in the Middle Ages and reached its height under King Tvrtko I in the 14th century. Bosnia had its own Christian church, and stećci, medieval decorated tombstones, are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Herzegovina, the southern region, takes its name from a 15th-century duke (herceg).

history.heading: Ottoman and Austro-Hungarian rule
paragraphs: The Ottoman Empire conquered Bosnia in 1463 and Herzegovina in 1482. Over four centuries many Bosnians converted to Islam, while Orthodox and Catholic Christians remained, and Sephardic Jews arrived from Spain. Sarajevo and Mostar flourished as Ottoman towns; Mostar's Old Bridge, built in 1566, became a symbol of the country.
Austria-Hungary occupied Bosnia in 1878 and annexed it in 1908. The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand by Gavrilo Princip in Sarajevo in 1914 triggered the First World War.

history.heading: Yugoslavia
paragraphs: Bosnia became part of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. During the Second World War it was incorporated into the fascist Independent State of Croatia, and the region saw mass killings and fierce partisan fighting. After the war it became one of six republics in socialist Yugoslavia under Tito. Sarajevo hosted the 1984 Winter Olympics.

history.heading: War and peace
paragraphs: Bosnia declared independence in 1992 after a referendum boycotted by most Serbs. A brutal war followed between Bosniaks, Serbs and Croats, with ethnic cleansing and the nearly four-year siege of Sarajevo. In July 1995, Bosnian Serb forces killed about 8,000 Bosniak men and boys at Srebrenica, a crime ruled to be genocide by international courts.

The Dayton Agreement of 1995 ended the war and created the current constitutional structure. About 100,000 people died and more than 2 million were displaced. Bosnia became an EU candidate country in 2022.

culture.heading: Peoples and religions
paragraphs: The three main groups are Bosniaks, mostly Muslim; Serbs, mostly Orthodox Christian; and Croats, mostly Catholic. Bosnian, Serbian and Croatian are mutually intelligible standard forms of the same language, written in Latin and Cyrillic scripts.
Sarajevo, with mosques, churches and synagogues close together, has been called the "Jerusalem of Europe".

culture.heading: Arts and food
paragraphs: Sevdalinka, a traditional form of melancholic love song, is central to Bosnian music. Ivo Andrić, author of The Bridge on the Drina, won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1961. The Sarajevo Film Festival is one of the largest in the region.
Popular dishes include ćevapi (grilled minced meat), burek, begova čorba (soup) and Bosnian coffee served in a džezva. Coffee drinking is an important social ritual.

politics.heading: The Dayton system
paragraphs: Bosnia and Herzegovina has one of the most complex political systems in the world. It consists of two entities, the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (mainly Bosniak and Croat) and Republika Srpska (mainly Serb), plus the self-governing Brčko District.

A three-member presidency rotates between a Bosniak, a Croat and a Serb. Each entity has its own government and parliament. An international High Representative oversees the peace agreement and can impose laws. Politics is often divided along ethnic lines, and Republika Srpska's leaders have repeatedly challenged state institutions and threatened secession.

politics.heading: European path
paragraphs: Joining the EU and NATO are official goals, though NATO membership is opposed by many Serbs. The EU agreed to open accession negotiations in 2024, conditional on reforms.

economy.heading: Economic structure
paragraphs: Bosnia's economy suffered greatly from the war and the transition from socialism. Key sectors include metal processing, energy (coal and hydropower), wood and furniture, and agriculture. Tourism is growing, especially in Sarajevo and Mostar.
The convertible mark is pegged to the euro. Remittances from the large diaspora are important. Challenges include high unemployment, corruption, a large public sector and emigration of young people.
